extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educators (physicists, chemists, astronomers, archaeologists) reading Nature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing short scientific reports, lecture demonstrations, observational notes, and archaeological classifications as published in a 19th-century scientific journal. Covers experimental demonstrations, laboratory/field methods, observational reporting, and typology/classification of antiquities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of magic-lantern slides to display vibration-lines
rubrics_metrics.description: For displaying the relation between the 'quality' of musical tones and the kind of vibration producing them, use magic-lantern slides prepared as smoked glass plates on which vibration-lines are traced by points attached to tuning-forks, piano-wires, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each tone should be sounded as its vibration-line is shown so the audience can appreciate differences (simple tone of tuning-fork vs clangs of a stringed instrument). Slides are simple and inexpensive means to illustrate important points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate irregular/discordant vibrations (Bismarck's Whistle)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show the relation of an irregularly discordant clang to an irregularly bent and jagged vibration-line, use an enlarged 'Bismarck's Whistle' (tin canister with a gut string) and take the vibration-line off on smoked glass from a pointed wire soldered to the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange a conspicuously irregular sound-making device and record its vibration-line for pictorial comparison with regular tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating beats with simple apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: If Helmholtz's membrane plan or Lissajous apparatus are not available, use two stout piano-wires stretched side by side on a board, connected near the middle by a bent yoke terminating in a point, tuned to give beats at a convenient rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a central pointer to show alternate phases of addition and subtraction corresponding to beats; take pictures of the beats on smoked glass to form slides. The method should be simpler/coarser but effective for lecture demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduated resonant-tube apparatus for class instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: A 4-ft length of 3-inch zinc tube nearly filled with water, with a 2-in. tube raised and lowered to resonate with a large tuning-fork, is a convenient means of demonstrating the principle of lengths of organ-pipes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used for class purposes, graduate the tube to quarters of an inch so pupils can practise calculating the wavelength and thence the pitch of a tuning-fork tested by the resonant tube.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing overtones of open pipes for demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-ft length of 1 in. iron gas tube serves well to produce the overtones of open pipes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit a trumpet mouth-piece at one end so the most elementary musical scale (simple trumpet-music) may be effectively given; this is useful for demonstrations of overtone series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualising vibrating rods or kaleidophone patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: When large-scale kaleidophone experiments cannot be displayed, use a lighted Chinese joss-stick attached to the end of an umbrella rib to show convoluted figures representing the path of the end of a vibrating rod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any bright permanent spark can be used; the plan also serves to show the path of a point on a long vibrating wire. Ensure the lighted spark is visible to the audience at a distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making vibrating forks' motion visible to audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix an inch of lighted joss-stick transversely near the end of one leg of a tuning-fork to show the contrast between the continuous line traced by waving the quiescent fork and the series of dots when the fork is waved while in vibration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to demonstrate how counteracting movements resolve the trace into dots; visibility at lecture distance is the key requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive 'scrubbing' in coal-gas purification
rubrics_metrics.description: Washing crude gas with water removes some sulphur (in the form of sulphide of ammonium) but excessive 'scrubbing' greatly deteriorates the gas's illuminating power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit aqueous washing; evaluate trade-off between impurity removal and loss of illuminating power when choosing purification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of sulphuretted hydrogen from coal gas
rubrics_metrics.description: Two commonly used methods for removing sulphuretted hydrogen are passing the gas over lime, and passing the gas over oxide of iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods are comparatively effective and it is stated to be rare to find H2S in gas as supplied to consumers when these purifiers are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposing bisulphide of carbon by heating with hydrogen
rubrics_metrics.description: Heating a mixture of bisulphide of carbon vapour and hydrogen to redness decomposes the former into sulphuretted hydrogen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After this conversion, passage through an iron purifier removes the sulphuretted hydrogen, making removal of bisulphide of carbon from coal gas possible by hot-tube treatment followed by iron purification. Experimental data show substantial reduction in sulphur content and sometimes increased illuminating power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing purification efficacy by quantitative measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate gas-purification processes by measuring grains of sulphur per 100 cubic feet and by measuring illuminating power in candles before and after treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paired measurements to demonstrate both impurity reduction (e.g., from 30 to ~5–6 grains per 100 cu ft) and any change (increase or decrease) in illuminating power after treatments such as heating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation and institutional support for observatory projects
rubrics_metrics.description: For establishing an observatory: form an association, seek advice from the Astronomer Royal about proper site and initiatory work, and secure governmental approval and financial support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a site with natural advantages and obtain subscriptions, grants, or endowment and governmental assistance for maintenance; coordinate with imperial/colonial authorities when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site selection criteria for astronomical observatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A favourable site lies between the ocean and mountain ranges where there is an expanse of unbroken plain with remarkable clearness of atmosphere, permitting observation of a much larger area of the heavens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess local geography (distance to ocean and mountains), atmospheric clarity, and the extent of level land when recommending sites for observational stations (e.g., for the Transit of Venus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modelling-wax plaster-casting method (materials and steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use artists' modelling wax as the mould material; cover the object with a thin powder of steatite or French chalk to prevent adhesion; soften wax by warm water or heat; apply and press into cavities; cut edges for multi-piece moulds; let wax cool until hard enough to repeat; extract original before the mould is perfectly cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Then pour wetted plaster of Paris (to prevent air bubbles), fill multi-piece moulds separately before assembling, dry casts wholly or partially, paint in water colours lighter than the original, steep the dried cast in hard paraffin, cool, and polish by hand with steatite. The method reproduces microscopic surface details and is inexpensive—suitable for making type-specimen casts for comparison and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tips for producing high-quality plaster casts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent air bubbles by wetting moulds; use steatite (French chalk) to prevent pieces of mould sticking; fill pieces of multi-part moulds separately before joining; remove original from mould before complete cooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint casts lighter than the original (because subsequent paraffin treatment will intensify colours); steep in paraffin to harden; polish with steatite to obtain good final surface comparable for comparison purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational reporting for nebulae and variable scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish occurrence of sensible changes in nebulae by using drawings, observing notes, and repeated observations with the same instrument; compare with historical drawings (e.g., Herschel) and note inapplicability where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record dates of drawings, instrument used (power), and observing conditions; note that higher powers on good nights reveal details invisible at lower powers; provide a series of dated drawings to document morphological changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectroscopic reporting caveats (nebulae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectral appearance can vary over time and depend on spectrographic setup: e.g., bright lines observed at one date may be absent later, and a wide slit may show absorption bands in positions of usual nebular lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report slit width and spectral setup when noting emission/absorption features and compare spectral observations across dates and instrument configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for persistent monitoring of variable astronomical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term, unremitting study of a nebula (or other variable astronomical region) is necessary; restricting attention to a specific vicinity is acceptable but labour-intensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a large field of labour; document incremental discoveries (e.g., increased number of 'stars' seen compared to earlier observers) and continue repeated high-power observations on good nights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish amorpholiths from hewn/sculptured stones in megalithic studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the rough shapeless blocks ('amorpholiths') of Carnac with the hewn and sculptured stones of Locmariaker; note sculptured stones, traces of coloured pigment, cup-markings, and different ornamentation styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use field evidence (sculpture traces, pigment, cup-markings) and mapping to separate monument classes; avoid sweeping generalisations in typology without noting local exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of illustrations beyond maps for megalithic monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps alone do not convey size and style; include views and drawings so readers who have not visited the site can appreciate the size and character of amorpholiths and alignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide perspective views and figures in addition to maps; the absence of illustrations may mislead or underrepresent the monuments' visual impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in mineral nomenclature for archaeological finds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accurate mineral names (e.g., jadeite and callais) instead of the broad terms 'jade' and 'turquoise' when curators or analysts identify specific materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow curator reports and mineralogical distinctions when describing material composition of artefacts to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material composition as a classificatory/crucial archaeological criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The predominance of fibrolite among celts in sepulchral dolmen-mounds (about 75% in cited table) is significant; fibrolite celts tend to be small, nearly perfect, sharp-edged, and show no signs of use, whereas diorite and larger celts show use and are broken before deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material and use-wear characteristics to infer deposition context (e.g., association with sepulture) and to classify implement types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dolmen-mounds typology (Types 1–12)
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed typology of dolmen-mounds and interior structures: (1) Long barrow (nil interior structure); (2) Round ditto, simple kist; (3) Ordinary megalithic dolmen, single chamber with passage; (4) Many-chambered megalithic dolmen with single narrow entrance; (5) Many-chambered with narrow entrance, megalithic and ceiled; (6) Long narrow megalithic chamber, sometimes divided, sometimes with dolmen entrance; (7) Round megalithic dolmen with passage at sharp angle with chamber and entrance descending into chamber; (8) Megalithic dolmen with curved gallery or passage; (9) Two or more megalithic dolmens parallel or at right angles; (10) Square megalithic chamber with long straight avenue and elaborate ornamentation; (11) Long ditto with other smaller kists, ceiled and vaulted; (12) Immense tumuli partly megalithic/ceiled/vaulted, often elliptical and containing kists and inhumation relics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the typology to classify observed monuments; give examples for each type (Kerlescant, Carnoet, Passiz, Keriaval, Le Rocher, Gavr' Inis, Manné-Lud, Mont S. Michel, etc.) and note frequency/rarity and distinguishing features (entrances, peristaliths, ornamentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify provenance and toponymy in archaeological reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure correct place-names, etymologies, and identifications (e.g., errors such as Aruhenho for Kercouno or Mahé vs Malé in references should be corrected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check local toponymy and earlier publications to avoid propagating errors; include trustworthy plans and elevations where appropriate to resolve disputes about composition (e.g., whether a menhir is fragmentary or a single monolith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative field evidence to test theories (e.g., post-Roman dating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject theories about origin/period (e.g., that dolmens date from a post-Roman period) to comparative field evidence, material analyses, and typological distinctions rather than accepting them uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and compare artefactual, structural, and contextual data across sites before endorsing chronological theories; correct unintentional misstatements and errata in prior works where necessary.
